日本[にほん]語[ご]の 料金[りょうきん] 案内[あんない]が 読[よ]めません
I can’t read the fare information in Japanese.
日本語 (にほんご, nihongo) means "Japanese," 料金 (りょうきん, ryōkin) means "fare," and 読めません (よめません, yomemasen) means "cannot read."

次 · じ · An ordinal number suffix usually combined with the ordinal number prefix 第 (だい), 次 expresses the order of events.
この 神[かみ]に、 氏名[しめい]、 電話[でんわ] 番号[ばんごう]、 住所[じゅうしょ]を 書[か]いてください
Please write your name, phone number, and address on this paper.

この (kono) means "this," 神 (かみ, kami) here refers to a paper/form where you write information. 氏名 (しめい, shimei) means "name," 電話番号 (でんわばんごう, denwa bangō) means "phone number," and 住所 (じゅうしょ, jūsho) means "address." 書いてください (かいてください, kaite kudasai) is a polite way of saying "please write."

個 · こ · Like 〜つ, you can count almost anything with this counter, though it's slightly less versatile. Think of it this way: if the thing you're counting has a boundary to it, you can use 個. If it doesn't have a distinct boundary, or it's too abstract, it's an age, or it's related to number order, it's more common to use 〜つ.
A polite way of saying "it's fine" or "it’s good enough." You can also use to mean "I'm fine" or "I've had enough."

もう (mō) means "already" or "no more," and 結構 (kekkō) means "enough" or "fine." です (desu) is a polite ending. This phrase is commonly used to politely decline further offers, such as when you don’t want more food, drink, or assistance. It conveys that you are satisfied or don’t need anything else.

お酒 (osake) means "alcohol" or "sake" (the Japanese rice wine). は (wa) is the topic marker, indicating that "alcohol" is the topic of the sentence. 結構 (kekkō) means "enough" or "fine," but in this context, it is used to politely decline something. です (desu) is the polite ending. This phrase is a polite way to refuse alcohol when offered.

A polite statement of how the customer intends to pay. 現金 (genkin) means "cash," で (de) indicates the method of payment, and お願いします (onegaishimasu) means "please," used for making a polite request.

1[いち]男[なん] 2[に]女[じょ]を 授[さず]かった。

女 · じょ · Daughters. It's read entirely with kango, except for two, which is read じ. 女 can also be an ordinal number suffix, in which case "one" is replaced with 長 (ちょう) to make 長女 (ちょうじょ) and indicate "first daughter." Similarly, "two" is replaced with 次 (じ) to make 次女 (じじょ) and indicate "second daughter".

完全に (かんぜんに, kanzen ni) means "completely." 迷ってしまいました (まよってしまいました, mayo tte shimaimashita) is the polite past form of 迷う (まよう, mayou), meaning "to get lost," with しまいました (shimaimashita) indicating a sense of regret or completion.

すみませんが、 これは 何[なん]の 金額[きんがく]ですか？
Excuse me, what is this amount?

すみません (sumimasen) is an expression of apology or attention, and これは (kore wa) means "this" (referring to something close to the speaker). 何の (なんの, nan no) means "what kind of," and 金額 (きんがく, kingaku) refers to "amount" or "sum." The sentence is asking about the amount of money, and the question marker か (ka) is used at the end.
マミの 成績[せいせき]は いつも クラスで ２[に]番[ばん]です。

番 · ばん · 番 is an ordinal number suffix to show one's order, turn, or rank. It is common for 番 to be combined with another ordinal number suffix, 目 (め): 一番目, 二番目, etc.

すみません (sumimasen) is a polite apology, もう一度 (mō ichido) means "once again," and 確かめてください (たしかめてください, tashikamete kudasai) is a polite request for confirmation.

Please show me my current location
現在地 (げんざいち, genzaichi) means "current location," and 示してください (しめしてください, shimeshite kudasai) means "please show."

園 · えん · Institutions that end with 園 or 園地 (えんち), such as zoos (動物園/どうぶつえん), botanical gardens (植物園/しょくぶつえん), theme parks (遊園地/ゆうえんち), gardens (庭園/ていえん), farms (農園/のうえん), orchards (果樹園/かじゅえん), kindergartens (幼稚園/ようちえん), or nursery schools/preschools (保育園/ほいくえん) all use the same counter. You'll see 園 mostly used in writing. When counting schools that use 学園 (がくえん), use either 学園 (がくえん) or 校 (こう) instead of just 園.

問 · もん · Questions or problems in a test, exam, quiz, textbook, etc. It can also be used with the ordinal number prefix 第 to indicate question number.

あなたが 欲[ほ]しい。
すべて 忘[わす]れたい。

困る (こまる, komaru) means "to be troubled" or "to be inconvenienced," and ません (masen) is the negative form, indicating that it is not a problem.
あなたは 暖[あたた]かい。

どこで 降[お]りますか？
どこ (doko) means "where." 降ります (おります, orimasu) is the polite form of "to get off" or "to descend." か (ka) turns it into a question.
すぐに 忘[わす]れられるよ。

The phrase uses the verb 探す (sagasu) in the ている (te-iru) form to express an ongoing action, like "ing" in English, indicating that you are in the process of looking for something.
ここで 降[お]ろしてください
で (de) indicates the place where the action will happen. 降ろして (おろして, oroshite) is the te-form of 降ろす (おろす, orosu), meaning "to drop (someone) off."

お座って (おすわって, osuwatte) is the te-form of 座る (suwaru), meaning "to sit." ください (kudasai) is a polite way of saying "please," forming a polite request.

何か (nanika) means "something," and お探し (osagashi) is the polite form of the verb 探す (sagasu), meaning "to look for." ですか (desu ka) turns the sentence into a polite question.

装い · よそい/よそおい · The counter 装い is used to count both servings (よそい) and sets of clothes, costumes, or furniture (よそおい).

この 席[せき]に 座[すわ]っていいですか？

この (kono) means "this," 席 (せき, seki) means "seat," and 座っていいですか (suwatte ii desu ka) is asking if it's okay to sit in the seat.
どの 席[せき]に 座[すわ]っていましたか？
Which seat were you sitting in?

どの (dono) means "which" and is used to ask about a specific item from a known set. 席 (せき, seki) means "seat." 座っていました (すわっていました, suwatte imashita) is the past continuous form of "to sit," indicating that someone was sitting at the time. か (ka) is the question marker, turning the sentence into a question.
あなたの 温[ぬく]もりが 忘[わす]れられなかった。
あなたの 優[やさ]しさが 忘[わす]れられなかった。
I couldn't forget how kind you are.
あそこの 人[ひと]が 並[なら]んでいる ところです。
That's where the people are lined up over there.

危険[きけん]を 感[かん]じる
頭[あたま]が 混乱[こんらん] する
これが 確認[かくにん]書[しょ]です
確認書 (かくにんしょ, kakuninsho) means "confirmation letter," and です (desu) is the copula.
困難[こんなん]に 打[う]ちのめされる
どんな 人[ひと]を 尊敬[そんけい] する？

荷物[にもつ]を 預[あず]けたいんですが
I would like to check in my luggage.
荷物 (にもつ, nimotsu) means "luggage," and 預けたい (あずけたい, azuketai) means "want to check in" or "want to leave."
あなたは 尊敬[そんけい] される 人[ひと]。
あなたを 一生[いっしょう]、 忘[わす]れない。
I'll never forget you, not for the rest of my life.
チケット 二[に]枚[まい] お願[ねが]いします
チケット (chiketto) means "ticket." 二枚 (にまい, nimai) means "two tickets" (枚 is the counter for flat objects). お願いします (おねがいします, onegaishimasu) is a polite way to say "please."
割引[わりびき] クーポンは 使[つか]えますか？
Can I use a discount coupon?
この 荷物[にもつ]を 預[あず]かってください
預かる (あずかる, azukaru) means "to hold onto" or "keep" something for someone, and ください (kudasai) is a polite request.
券売[けんばい] 機[き]で チャージ できますよ。
You can charge it at the ticket machine.
その 店[みせ]は 駅[えき]の 裏[うら]に ありますよ。
That store is behind the station.
おにぎりは 冷蔵[れいぞう]庫[こ]に あります。
The onigiri is in the refrigerator.
Similar to the previous sentence, this uses あります (arimasu) to describe the existence of the onigiri in the refrigerator.
